January 8, 2026 - Testimony in support of LD 2033:
Resolve, to Designate Route 3 in Trenton as the Deputy Luke Gross Memorial Highway
Good morning, Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts, and members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Transportation. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.
My name is Representative Billy Bob Faulkingham. I serve as the House Republican Leader and
represent House District 12, which includes Franklin, Gouldsboro, Hancock, Sorrento, Sullivan,
Winter Harbor, and Steuben. I am here today in support of my proposed legislation, LD 2033, a
resolve to designate Route 3 in Trenton as the Deputy Luke Gross Memorial Highway.
LD 2033 is a simple and straightforward resolve directing the Department of Transportation to
designate a portion of Route 3 in the Town of Trenton in Deputy Gross's honor, the location where
he sacrificed his life in the line of duty, and to erect fitting signage. The proposal will not alter any traffic patterns or impose any regulatory requirements. Instead, it provides a lasting and
meaningful tribute to a public servant who gave his life in service to the people of Maine.
Deputy Luke Gross served with the Hancock County Sheriff's Office for 18 years. He was a dedicated law enforcement officer, a committed public servant, and a person of strong character. His death in the line of duty in November 2022 was a profound loss for his family, his fellow officers, and the entire Hancock County community.
Luke is survived by his wife, Lauren, and their two children, Ryan and Alissa. A graduate of Bucksport High School, he proudly wore jersey number 80 for the Golden Bucks football team. He
attended the University of Maine at Augusta and graduated from the Maine Criminal Justice Academy.
Beyondhis law enforcement career, Luke was deeply engaged in his community. He volunteered
as a camp counselor at Camp Postcard, served as a DARE officer for Hancock County, and was
actively involved in fundraising efforts for Hancock County Sheriff's Charities.
Route 3 in Trenton is an appropriate location for this designation. It is a we|l--traveled corridor in
Hancock County and one familiar to residents, visitors, and members of the law enforcement community. Naming this highway in Deputy Gross's honor will serve as an enduring reminder of
his service and of the risks faced each day by our law enforcement officers and first responders.

Memorial highway designations are one way the Maine Legislature can recognize and honor individuals who have made extraordinary sacrifices for our communities. This resolve ensures that Deputy Gross's name and legacy are preserved in a respectful and dignified manner, while offering his family and colleagues a permanent acknowledgment of his service.
I respectfully ask the Committee to support LD 2033 and report the bill out "Ought to Pass." Thank you for your time and consideration. l would be happy to answer any questions.
Respectfully,

Testimony of Meghan Russo Maine Department of Transportation
Before the 132"" Legislature, Joint Standing Committee on Transportation
Neither for Nor Against LD 2033
Resolve, to Designate Route 3 in Trenton as the Deputy Luke Gross Memorial Highway
Senator Nangle-, Representative Crafts and distinguished members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Transportation, I am Meghan Russo, Director of Government Affairs at
MaineDOT. MaineDOT is neither for nor against LD 2033.
MaineDOT considers the naming of bridges, roadways, and other state transportation infrastructure to be within the purview of the Legislature. Simply put, we build them and you name them. Accordingly, we generally do not take positions on so-called "naming bills." However, we usually submit written testimony regarding whether the particular infrastructure under consideration has been named before, and if so what those name(s) are. In this case, we
are not aware of any previous legislatively-sanctioned names for this section of roadway.
Thank you.

Testimony ofSenator Nicole Grohoski and Representative Nina Milliken in support of
LD 2033, Resolve, to Designate Route 3 in Trenton as the
Deputy Luke Gross Memorial Highway
Before the Committee on Transportation January 8, 2026
Good aftemoon, Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts, and distinguished members of the
Transportation Committee. We are Senator Nicole Grohoski, representing Senate District 7, and Representative Nina Milliken, representing House District 16. Together, we represent the town of Trenton, where Deputy Luke Gross lost his life on September 23, 2021. We are pleased to present testimony in support of LD 2033, "Resolve, to Designate Route 3 in Trenton as the Deputy Luke
Gross Memorial Highway."
On that September morning nearly four and a half years ago, Deputy Luke Gross was doing what comprises so much of an officer's job--sorting out someone else's mess. He was clearing debris
from an accident scene on Route 3, his cruiser's emergency lights activated, wearing a reflective
safety vest. He bent down to pick something up from the road. He was struck from behind and
died of his injuries.
The loss shook our entire region. Deputy Gross was 44 years old, a Bucksport native, a proud
father to Ryan and Alissa, and devoted husband to Lauren. But here in Hancock County, we knew him as so much more. He was the deputy who brought smiles to kids` faces at Christmas
through Sheriffs Office fundraisers. He was the DARE officer in our schools and a counselor at Camp POSTCARD (Police Officers Striving to Create and Reinforce Dreams). He was the friend
who drove a colleague battling cancer to Boston for treatments, repeatedly, and without hesitation. He was the school board chairman at Hancock Grammar School who helped develop
the backpack program to feed children living with food insecurity.
As one colleague put it, Deputy Luke Gross was a big kid at heart who always tried to find the good in anything. He treated people warmly, with respect and a smile. He cared deeply about our
community.
Route 3 in Trenton is where Deputy Gross made the ultimate sacrifice while protecting public safety. Every day, thousands of residents and visitors travel that stretch of road on their way to

his compassion, and his dedication to others are not forgotten. It would remind all of us driving
that route to slow down, move over, and watch out for the first responders who put themselves at
risk to keep us safe.
The Ellsworth Area Chamber of Commerce posthumously named Luke their Citizen of the Year in 2022. Sheriff Scott Kane retired his call sign, Han9, ensuring no other deputy would ever be assigned that number. These were fitting tributes. This memorial highway designation would be another --- one that honors him in the very place where he fell, and one that carries forward his
legacy every single day.
We would like to conclude by noting that our absence as cosponsors should in no way be
interpreted as anything other than an oversight by the bill sponsor. Had we been approached to cosponsor this bill, we would have been honored to do so. Trenton is our community, and Deputy
Luke Gross served our neighbors in Trenton and around Hancock County with distinction for 18 years. Thank you for allowing us the opportunity to make our support of this bill absolutely clear.
We hope you will join us in doing so. Thank you.

Good morning, Madam Chair Crafts, Mr. Chair Nangle, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Transportation. Thank you for allowing me to speak.
For the record, my name is Scott Kane, and l serve as the Sheriff of Hancock County.
I am here today not only as a law enforcement professional, but as someone who had the
privilege of working alongside Deputy Gross, and of knowing Luke as a person.
On September 23, 2001, at 5:01 in the morning, Luke was struck by a vehicle while performing
his duties. At 5:03 A.l\/l., I received a call notifying me that Luke had been hit. That moment is burned into my memory -- and it marks the beginning of a moment that permanently changed
our office, our community, and a family whose lives were forever altered.
Luke was the kind of officer every agency hopes for and every community deserves. He was dependable, steady, and took his responsibility to serve others seriously. But what truly set him
apart was who he was beyond the uniform. Luke was kind. He was caring. And despite the weight of this profession, he was still a kid at heart --- someone who could bring lightness,
laughter, and humanity into even the hardest days.
He had a way of making people feel at ease. He made people feel safe. And he made the people around him better -- simply by being who he was.
His loss left a space that cannot be filled --- in our department, in our community, and most
especially in the hearts of his family. We carry his name in our memories, but his family carries
his absence every day.
Designating this portion of Route 3 as the Luke Gross Memorial Highway is more than a sign on the side of the road. it is a public acknowledgment that Luke mattered -- that his service mattered --- and that his life continues to be honored in the very place where he served and
protected others.
it gives his family something permanent. Something visible. Something that says: Luke's life, his character, and his sacrifice are not forgotten.
For those of us who worked with Luke, it also gives us a place to pause --- to remember why we wear this badge, why integrity matters, and why service is more than just a job.
This designation would mean a great deal to our office. But more importantly, it would mean a great deal to his family -- and to a community that is better because Luke was part of it.
Thank you for your time, and thank you for considering this. I would be happy to answer any
questions the Committee may have.

Statement in support of
L.D. 2033, Resolve, to Designate Route 3 in Trenton as the Deputy Luke Gross Memorial Highway
Joint Standing Committee on Transportation
January 8, 2026
Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts, and honorable members of the Transportation Committee. My name is Scott Stewart. I am the Chief of the Brunswick Police Department, and the newly elected President of the Maine Chiefs of Police Association. I am submitting testimony on behalf of the Association in support of LD 2033.
The Maine Chiefs of Police Association's mission is straightforward: to strengthen the working relationships among Maine's police leaders, to promote professionalism and consistent standards across the state, and to support the men and women who serve our communities every day. At the heart of that mission is a shared commitment to protecting life and property and upholding the values of our profession.
Deputy Luke Gross was not a member of our Association, but that has never mattered when it comes to how we view our law enforcement family. In Maine, we stand together. When one agency loses an officer, every department feels that loss. Deputy Gross served Hancock County for 18 years with quiet dedication and a genuine concern for the people he encountered. His work as a DARE officer and his steady presence in the community made a lasting impact on many.
In 2021, Deputy Gross was killed while doing something officers do countless times without recognition, clearing debris from the road so others would be safe. Sheriff Scott Kane called him "a credit to his profession" and said the world needs more people like him. Those words resonated across the state because they were true.

Naming this stretch of Route 3 in his honor is a fitting way to remember his service and sacrifice. It ensures that his legacy remains visible in the community he served, and it reminds all of us of the risks officers take every day on behalf of the public.
For these reasons, the Maine Chiefs of Police Association respectfully urges the Committee to support LD 2033.

Thank you, Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts, and members of the
Transportation Committee.
I am Representative Steve Bishop. I represent District 17, which is the towns of Orland, Penobscot, Verona Island, and my hometown of Bucksport.
Thank you for the opportunity to speak today in support of naming this road in honor of Deputy Luke Gross of the Hancock County Sheriff' s Office.
Luke Gross was not only a dedicated law enforcement officer, but also a mentor, a
leader, and a friend. Early in my law enforcement career, Luke and I worked
together. As a young officer, I quickly came to respect and admire him, not only
for his professionalism, but for the way he carried himself every day. He was
someone I looked up to, someone whose example helped shape the law enforcement officer I became.
Luke was kind, compassionate, and genuinely generous in how he treated people. He had a rare ability to connect with others, whether they were victims, coworkers, students, or complete strangers. He didn't just enforce the law, he served the
community with empathy and patience, always taking the time to treat people with dignity and respect. Those qualities earned him the trust of the public and the deep
respect of those who worked alongside him.
He was especially passionate about the D.A.R.E. program and devoted a great deal
of time and energy to working with young people throughout Hancock County.
Luke cared deeply about the next generation. He believed in guiding, teaching, and
protecting our youth, and he understood that strong relationships between law
enforcement and schools are essential to building safer communities. He was a
leader in our schools, just as he was a leader in law enforcement.
